terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. `node src/offers.ts` runs the offers, and `npm run types` checks their types.

tasks.title: Write the type of a callback
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/offers.ts`, `labelAll` takes a list of blends and `format`, a function that takes one blend (text) and gives back its label (text). Write the type of `format`. Leave the body as it is.

Check refuses `any` and `as` in your lines, and reads `labelAll` for its result type. It compiles calls of its own: a function from a blend to text must be accepted, with its parameter typed or not, while a function that gives back a number, one that takes a number, or text in place of a function must be refused. It calls `labelAll` with blends and a function of its own.
nextSteps: Run `npm run types` and read the errors: which one is about `format`, and which are about the callback below it?
Write the type of `format` after its name: the parameter it takes in round brackets, an arrow, and the type it gives back.
Run `npm run types` again: the error on the callback below goes too.
Run `node src/offers.ts` and look at the labels.
hints: `Parameter 'format' implicitly has an 'any' type` is the same message as for any other parameter without a type. A function is a value, so its parameter gets a type like any other.
A function type is written like an arrow function with types and no body: the parameters in round brackets with their types, then `=>`, then the type of what it gives back.

tasks.title: Give a price rule a name
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a type alias called `PriceRule`, with `export` in front: a function that takes a price in pence (a number) and gives back a new price in pence (a number). Use it as the type of `fridayOff`, and in the type of `rules` on `applyRules`: a list of price rules. Leave the bodies as they are.

Check refuses `any` and `as` in your lines. It reads your lines for the word `type` in front of `PriceRule`, for `PriceRule` on `fridayOff` and `applyRules`, and for the result type of `applyRules`. It compiles code of its own: rules made with `PriceRule` and a list of them passed to `applyRules` must compile, while a rule that gives back text, a rule that takes text or one rule where a list goes must be refused. It calls `fridayOff`, and `applyRules` with rules of its own.
nextSteps: Write the type alias above `fridayOff`: `export type`, the name, `=`, and a function type.
Write the name after `fridayOff`, with a colon, and read what happens to the error on `pence`.
Write the type of `rules`: a list of that type.
hints: A type alias can name any type, a function type included. Once it has a name, a variable, a parameter or a list can use it.
With the alias on the variable, the compiler knows what the arrow function takes, so `pence` needs no type of its own. A list of rules is the alias followed by `[]`.
`export type PriceRule = (pence: number) => number`, then `export const fridayOff: PriceRule = ...` and `rules: PriceRule[]`.

tasks.title: Pass the position every time
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, `numbered` takes a list of lines and `format`, a function that takes a line (text) and its position in the list counting from 1 (a number), and gives back text. `numbered` always passes both. Some callbacks use only the line, and Bryn's uses the position too. Write the type of `format` so that both are accepted, and leave the body as it is.

Check refuses `any`, `as` and a `!` after a value in your lines, and reads `numbered` for its result type. It compiles calls of its own: a callback that uses only the line, and one that uses the position as a number, must compile, while a callback that gives back a number, one whose line is a number, or one that needs a third value must be refused. It calls `numbered` with lines and callbacks of its own.
nextSteps: Write the type of `format` with the two parameters it is always given.
Run `npm run types`. Does the callback that takes only the line still compile?
If Bryn's callback is refused, read the lesson's part on callbacks that take fewer values.
Run `node src/offers.ts` and look at the numbered lines.
hints: A function that takes fewer parameters fits a function type with more. JavaScript passes the extra values, and the function ignores them.
A question mark on a parameter of a callback type means `numbered` might not pass it, so every callback has to deal with `undefined`. `numbered` always passes the position, so it is not optional.
`format: (line: string, position: number) => string`, with no question mark.

tasks.title: Write a function that makes rules
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, write a function called `percentOff`, with `export` in front, from the word `function` to its closing brace. It takes a percent (a number) and gives back a price rule: a function that takes a price in pence and gives back that price less the percent, rounded to a whole penny with `Math.round`. `percentOff(10)` gives a rule that turns `1250` into `1125`. Write every type, the type of the function it gives back included. Then take away the `//` in front of the lines at the end, to see it run.

Check refuses `any` and `as` in your lines, and reads `percentOff` for its result type. It compiles code of its own: what `percentOff` gives back must be usable as a function from pence to pence, while a percent as text, pence as text, a price used as text, or the price passed to `percentOff` itself must be refused. It makes rules of its own with `percentOff` and calls them, two rules side by side among them.
nextSteps: Write the first line: the name, a percent parameter with its type, and as the result type a function type from pence to pence.
In the body, give back an arrow function that takes the pence.
Inside it, work out the price less the percent and round it.
Take away the `//` in front of the last lines, and run both commands.
hints: A function can give back a function, like any other value. The result type after the round brackets is then a function type, written as in Task 1.
The arrow function you give back can use `percent`, because it was made inside `percentOff`. Each call of `percentOff` makes a new rule with its own percent.
`export function percentOff(percent: number): (pence: number) => number {`, then `return (pence) => Math.round((pence * (100 - percent)) / 100)`.
